extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing novelists / professional authors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance on writing novels, magazine pieces, and managing a literary career (characterisation, style, revision, productivity, contracts, and remuneration). Drawn from an author's autobiographical reflections and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy — commit to one side
rubrics_metrics.description: Any writer in advocating a cause must do so after the fashion of an advocate; he should take up one side and cling to that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to argue both sides simultaneously when advocating — "Such scruples make a man impotent for such work." For effective persuasive writing, adopt one clear stance and pursue it without vacillation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating vice to satirize it (no manufactured caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire, though it may exaggerate the vice it lashes, is not justified in creating it in order that it may be lashed. Caricature may too easily become a slander, and satire a libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invent or grossly exaggerate faults simply to attack them; this risks libel, slander, and ethical compromise. Keep satire grounded in truth and avoid fabricating vice for rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not combine contradictory objectives in one work
rubrics_metrics.description: The two objects (exposing ecclesiastical malversation and defending undeserving clerical victims) should not have been combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to serve opposing aims (e.g., both to attack institutional abuse and to defend individuals) in the same narrative — choose a single dominant purpose for clarity and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation — produce clear, recognisable portraits
rubrics_metrics.description: The characters ... are all well and clearly drawn. I had realised to myself a series of portraits, and had been able so to put them on the canvas that my readers should see that which I meant them to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong fiction depends on the author's ability to visualise and render characters so readers 'see' them. Cultivate the skill of producing distinct, coherent portraits on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and grammar — good English plus care with grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: The style of the English was good, though from most unpardonable carelessness the grammar was not unfrequently faulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a good literary style but attend to grammatical correctness; careless grammar undermines otherwise strong prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective acceptance of editorial criticism; resist destructive cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: I went through the criticisms, rejecting one and accepting another, almost alternately, but declaring at last that no consideration should induce me to cut out a third of my work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial suggestions individually. Accept useful critiques but refuse demands (e.g., drastic cuts) that would destroy the integrity or meaning of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient writing habits — use travel time and simple tools
rubrics_metrics.description: I made for myself therefore a little tablet, and found after a few days' exercise that I could write as quickly in a railway-carriage as I could at my desk. I worked with a pencil, and what I wrote my wife copied afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop practical routines and tools (portable tablet, pencil) to write productively in varied settings; delegate mechanical tasks (copying) when possible to increase output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not compromise quality for money — honesty in authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: If indeed a man writes his books badly ... because he can make his money faster in that fashion ... he is dishonest, as is any other fraudulent dealer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standards even when financial incentives tempt you to produce inferior work. Selling 'shoddy for broadcloth' is dishonest and will be discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair remuneration and the importance of copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Brains that are unbought will never serve the public much. Take away from English authors their copyrights, and you would very soon take away from England her authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should seek fair payment and protection of rights; reasonable remuneration sustains literature and allows authors to serve the public effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-discipline — be severe with yourself about scamped work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a danger as to which he is bound to be severe with himself--in which he should feel that his conscience should be set fairly in the balance against the natural bias of his interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must honestly judge when enough labour has been given; resist scamping tasks due to personal bias or convenience and apply strict self-editing standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and learning while writing — pick up knowledge as you go
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing about clergymen generally, I had to pick up as I went whatever I might know or pretend to know about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about unfamiliar milieus or professions, learn by doing: gather needed facts and nuance during the writing process to enhance authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiating publishing terms — weigh lump sums vs half-profits and imprint value
rubrics_metrics.description: I argued with him that as soon as an author has put himself into a position which insures a sufficient sale ... the publisher is not entitled to expect the half of such proceeds ... 'It is for you,' said he, 'to think whether our names on your title-page are not worth more to you than the increased payment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate contracts understanding the trade-off between immediate payment and publisher prestige/long-term arrangements. Be aware of marketability when arguing for different terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid thinly veiled real-person portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: Tom Towers ... I had not even heard the name of any gentleman connected with the Times newspaper, and could not have intended to represent any individual by Tom Towers. As I had created an archdeacon, so had I created a journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when fictional characters resemble real individuals; readers and contemporaries may assume direct identification. Make creations sufficiently fictionalized to avoid mistaken identification or offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect variable payment for magazine articles
rubrics_metrics.description: He [proprietor] told me that such articles were generally written to oblige friends, and that articles written to oblige friends were not usually paid for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume magazine articles will be paid; terms vary and some pieces (especially favors) may be unpaid. Clarify payment expectations before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration often comes from travel and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whilst wandering there one midsummer evening round the purlieus of the cathedral I conceived the story of The Warden ... I made out to my own satisfaction the spot on which Hiram's hospital should stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use travel, place, and direct observation as sources of plot ideas, settings, and concrete details that can spark the opening of a work.
